rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient to locate all six peaks while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. The retention window and critical resolutions will guide subsequent gradient trimming and selectivity optimization.

Injection 1 already achieved the maximum CRF of 1.000. Shorten the gradient by one grid step to seek a faster fully resolved method while measuring how the critical pair responds to gradient steepness.
Shorten the gradient another step while holding the solvent window and temperature fixed. The minimum resolution of 3.24 leaves substantial margin to preserve the maximum CRF in a faster run.

The critical-pair resolution has decreased predictably with shorter gradients; extrapolation suggests a 4-minute gradient may still exceed R = 1.5. Test this next step to reduce run time while retaining the maximum CRF.

The 4-minute gradient retains maximum CRF but leaves little resolution margin for the first pair. Test the highest temperature to shorten retention and determine whether temperature improves or worsens that pair’s selectivity.

Higher temperature worsened the critical pair, so test the lowest temperature to increase its separation while shortening the gradient to 2 minutes. This probes whether improved temperature selectivity can support a faster fully resolved method; injection 4 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-CRF method.

Narrow the gradient window to reduce steepness and improve the first pair’s resolution while retaining the 2-minute gradient. The new starting fraction remains below the first peak’s estimated elution fraction of 0.33, and the high final fraction protects against delayed elution of the last compound.

Increase the starting organic fraction by one grid step to seek a shorter fully resolved run at the minimum gradient duration. Monitor the first pair closely, since earlier elution may offset the resolution benefit of the shallower gradient.

Raise temperature by one grid step to shorten the run while testing whether the first pair’s resolution margin is sufficient. Injection 8 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method if the temperature increase reduces resolution below 1.5.

Test one higher starting organic fraction to seek a further time reduction without sacrificing maximum CRF. The first peak is already close to the unretained region, so this injection checks whether early-peak compression sets the useful upper limit on phi0.

Return phi0 to 0.30 to avoid the early-peak compression seen at 0.35, and test one temperature step above the fastest fully resolved method. This checks the temperature boundary for maintaining maximum CRF at the minimum gradient duration.

Reduce the final organic fraction to make the gradient shallower and attempt to restore the first pair to R ≥ 1.5 at 35 C. This tests whether a narrower solvent window can compensate for temperature-induced selectivity loss without substantially delaying the last peak.

Lower phi0 to retain the first pair longer and make its separation more responsive to the gradient; reducing phi1 alone barely improved it. This tests whether the narrower window can recover full resolution at 35 C while keeping the run short.

Reduce phi1 one more step to spread the gradient-retained first pair, whose resolution is now close to 1.5. This seeks to recover maximum CRF at 35 C; injection 9 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-score method.

Return to the temperature and starting fraction of the fastest confirmed fully resolved method, but lower phi1 one step to test a modest resolution–time tradeoff. Injection 14 is borderline despite its rounded score, so prioritize a clear resolution margin over that apparent tie.

Test whether lowering temperature restores the early-pair separation lost at phi0 = 0.35 and 30 C. This checks the high-starting-organic boundary at the minimum gradient duration; injection 9 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-CRF method.

Return phi0 to 0.30 to avoid early-peak compression and lower temperature to strengthen the critical pair’s selectivity. This should provide a larger resolution margin at maximum CRF while retaining a short run; injection 9 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

The maximum CRF is already secured; test a lower starting fraction to keep the earliest peak away from the unretained region while preserving the shortest gradient. This checks whether full resolution persists on the lower-phi0 side of the successful 0.25–0.30 window.

Test a slightly narrower gradient at 30 C to retain the first pair beyond the near-unretained region while seeking full resolution. This explores a neighboring maximum-CRF method; injection 9 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved option.

Lower temperature one step from injection 19 to increase the critical pair’s resolution margin while keeping the first peak clearly retained. The maximum CRF is already secured, and injection 9 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Raise phi1 one step from injection 19 to shorten the last peak’s retention while checking whether the critical pair retains full resolution. This completes a close comparison around the fastest maximum-CRF region without repeating a method.

Use a shallower gradient at the temperature most favorable to the critical pair to seek a larger resolution margin while keeping all peaks well within 10 minutes. The maximum CRF is already achieved, with injection 9 still the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Raise temperature one step from injection 22 to shorten retention while using its resolution margin to preserve maximum CRF. This refines the narrow-window alternative; injection 9 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Increase phi0 one step from injection 23 to seek a shorter run while retaining full resolution, as this change helped at phi1 = 0.90 and 0.95. The maximum CRF is already secured; injection 9 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.
